extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; readers studying U.S. newspaper development
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative criteria and standards used to judge or design American newspapers (chiefly 1870s-1890s): content, format, business model, editorial practice, and organization. Useful for assessing historical newspapers or comparing contemporary practices to that era's standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as the heart of the paper
rubrics_metrics.description: “Modern in his conviction that news was the heart of the paper, he began his little Star with no less than seven reporters... The reporter is the essential man on the newspaper.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize vigorous news-gathering staff; prioritize original reporting as central to a paper's success rather than relying solely on editors or reprints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter qualities: honesty, accuracy, independence
rubrics_metrics.description: “He must be honest and accurate. At the same time he must never be a machine. Many reporters are ruined by allowing themselves to become messengers of the city editor. They cover assignments, and that is all they do.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should combine accuracy and integrity with initiative; avoid rote coverage and be encouraged to pursue leads and original angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and content for cheap afternoon papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern: “small size, entertaining human-interest materials, succinct writing, and the crusading spirit.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cheap afternoon papers succeeded by compact format, brisk writing, human-interest pieces, and an advocacy (crusading) element. Sensationalism may be optional depending on editorial choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance (or selective use) of sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding the Kansas City Star: “The element which was missing was sensationalism.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some successful papers deliberately avoided sensationalism, favoring civic crusades and community service; editors should decide stance on sensational content relative to mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crusading/public-service campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Long, persistent campaigns for city improvements, anti-corruption, regulation of street-railways, parks and boulevards; Nelson published “a total of 360 pages of matter in connection with this one campaign.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained investigative and advocacy campaigns are a measure of a paper's civic role; commitment may be measured in volume of coverage, resources devoted, and willingness to take legal/organizational steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paternalistic/community watchdog role
rubrics_metrics.description: The Star “made the Star the mentor and monitor of Kansas City. It was paternalistic; it looked after the interests of its readers as few newspapers have.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers may adopt a paternalistic stance—actively shaping citizens' tastes and civic priorities—through editorial advocacy, consumer campaigns, and guidance on daily life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rewards and private detectives in public-service work
rubrics_metrics.description: “The paper offered rewards for the arrest and conviction of the boodlers, and employed its own detectives... offered a reward for [Frank and Jesse James'] capture.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers sometimes used extrajudicial tactics (rewards, private investigation) to pursue civic goals; this reflects an activist model of journalism but raises ethical/legal considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence and political stance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Star “supported Cleveland and hard money, but was independent of party control” and was described as “genuinely mugwump.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial pages should disclose and balance political positions; independence from party machines can be a deliberate criterion for credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment in reporters and newsroom resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Nelson’s Star began with seven reporters; Hearst’s Examiner spent money on a large staff, special trains to cover events, and first-class features and art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure a paper's commitment by staffing levels and willingness to invest in news-gathering logistics (special trains, correspondents, feature staff).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of syndicates and feature distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Irving Bacheller (1883) and Samuel S. McClure pioneered syndicates making stories, household departments, and letters available to small papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Syndication is a quality/efficiency strategy—provides literary and feature material to smaller outlets; choice and reputation of syndicate affect perceived quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent insides / boiler plate for country weeklies
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooperative 'patent insides' and 'boiler plate' supplied readyprints to country papers; initial metal payment then use cost as low as twenty-five cents a column.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using syndicated preprinted material reduced costs but could affect local distinctiveness; assess trade-off between economy and editorial originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sunday edition richness: variety, sparkle, and illustration
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulitzer's Sunday World became a twenty-page paper 'running over with attractive news stories and features, some sensational, most light and readable, and all illustrated more fully than any newspaper had ever been before.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful Sunday paper combines variety of features, heavy illustration/art, readable light copy, and sometimes sensational items; size (pages) and illustration are key metrics of ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sunday papers as newspaper + literary miscellany
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘American journalism... is at once a newspaper and a literary miscellany, a society journal and household magazine.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sunday editions should blend news with longer-form literary and household material to serve multiple household readership functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature sections targeted to demographics
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature material designed for youth, women, followers of sports, the socialite, etc., commonly appeared in Sunday papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segmented features (women's columns, youth content, sports) increase audience reach; editors should curate features for target reader groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of star columnists and specialized columns
rubrics_metrics.description: Syndicated humorists and serious columns (Bill Nye, John A. Cockerill, Foster Coates, Helen Watterson) and women's columns were central features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hiring or syndicating prominent writers/columns builds readership and brand; quantity and reputation of columnists are metrics of editorial quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early comic features and proto comic strips
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic drawings and a sequence of drawings dealing with a single comic incident appeared in Sunday papers; the first regular comic section began in the New York World late in 1889.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual humor and sequential art are valuable reader attractions; innovation in recurring characters evolves into modern comic strips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance local/regional focus with national/international coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The Star was 'essentially local' yet 'gave fairly adequate news coverage in the national and international fields' after acquiring an A. P. franchise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong local reporting combined with wire service access (AP franchise) enables comprehensive coverage; securing news-service affiliations is an operational criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price and circulation strategies for growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-cent (penny) pricing and weekly subscription models: Star sold at two cents or ten cents a week; country papers charged $1–$2 annually; Sunday World raised price from three to five cents without much effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low unit price plus subscription options drive mass circulation; monitor price elasticity and circulation growth when altering price points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weekly editions compiled from dailies to expand reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Many dailies published weekly editions made up chiefly from material already published in dailies; some weeklies reached large circulations (Tribune, World, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producing weekly compilations leverages daily content to reach different markets; useful metric: weekly circulation vs daily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease of starting vs difficulty of maintaining country weeklies
rubrics_metrics.description: It took little capital to start a weekly in a small town (old presses, type, readyprint); but maintenance was difficult, producing migratory proprietors who moved from town to town.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Barriers to entry were low but economic sustainability was challenging; assess plant costs, credit arrangements, and working capital as key operational criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of advertising, art, and business investment to build circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Herald increased pages and built a fine building; Hearst spent on staff, trains, features, art, and parties which helped circulation growth; Sunday papers' advertising volumes were large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investment in presentation (art, building), promotional spending, and sales/advertising infrastructure are important drivers of growth and profitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial quality as reputation driver
rubrics_metrics.description: Harvey W. Scott’s editorial page (scholarly reading, forceful writing, high ideal of press responsibility) gave the Oregonian its reputation despite modest circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A distinguished editorial voice can confer prestige and influence beyond raw circulation numbers; assess depth, reasoning, and consistency of editorial opinion.
